scenes.animation: A school lab. Zippy mixes baking soda and vinegar in an open beaker on a weighing balance; it fizzes and the reading drops. Zippy gasps and points: 'Mass is disappearing!'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo! The reaction ate some mass! The balance reading went down!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Nothing was eaten. A gas escaped into the air. Close the flask and weigh again.

scenes.animation: Sepia portraits appear: 'Antoine L. Lavoisier' and 'Joseph L. Proust'. Title: 'Laws of Chemical Combination'. Then the law writes itself: 'Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Antoine Lavoisier laid the foundation of chemical sciences by establishing two important laws of chemical combination.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The first is the law of conservation of mass. It states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

scenes.animation: Activity built step by step: a conical flask holds sodium sulphate solution, and a small ignition tube of barium chloride solution hangs inside by a thread. The cork is fitted and the flask is weighed. The flask is tilted so the solutions mix and a white precipitate forms; the balance reading stays the same.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Take sodium sulphate solution in a conical flask. Hang a small tube of barium chloride solution inside it, and cork the flask. Weigh it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now tilt the flask so the two mix. A white precipitate forms, so a reaction has taken place. Weigh it again.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Same reading! Nothing escaped this time.

scenes.animation: Worked example on a blackboard, line by line: 'Q: 5.3 g sodium carbonate + 6 g ethanoic acid → 2.2 g CO2 + 0.9 g water + 8.2 g sodium ethanoate', 'Reactants: 5.3 + 6.0 = 11.3 g', 'Products: 2.2 + 0.9 + 8.2 = 11.3 g', '11.3 g = 11.3 g ✓ Law verified'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A textbook numerical. 5.3 grams of sodium carbonate reacts with 6 grams of ethanoic acid. The products are 2.2 grams of carbon dioxide, 0.9 grams of water and 8.2 grams of sodium ethanoate.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mass of reactants is 5.3 plus 6, which is 11.3 grams.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mass of products is 2.2 plus 0.9 plus 8.2. That is 3.1 plus 8.2, also 11.3 grams.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Both are equal, so the observations agree with the law of conservation of mass.

scenes.animation: Back to Zippy's first experiment: now in a closed bottle with a balloon on top. The balloon inflates with gas and the balance reading stays constant. A yellow 'EXAM TIP' sticker: 'Show total mass of reactants and products separately, then compare'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In your open beaker, carbon dioxide escaped. Trap it with a balloon, and the mass stays constant.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in these numericals, write the reactant total and product total on separate lines, then state the conclusion in words. That earns full marks.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a weighing balance icon. Points appear: '1. Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction', '2. Verify with a closed flask', '3. Mass of reactants = mass of products (11.3 g = 11.3 g)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: verify it in a closed flask, so no gas escapes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: total mass of reactants always equals total mass of products.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Mass is like my pocket money. It never disappears, it just goes somewhere else.

scenes.animation: Two glasses of water: one from a Himalayan spring, the other from a tap in Chennai. Zippy holds them up like trophies, sure they must be different.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Mountain water and Chennai tap water must have different recipes, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pure water from anywhere has the same recipe. Hydrogen and oxygen, always in the same ratio by mass.

scenes.animation: The law appears: 'In a chemical substance, the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass' with 'Law of constant proportions / law of definite proportions, stated by Proust'. A glass of water splits into two stacks: '1 g hydrogen : 8 g oxygen' from '9 g water'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Proust stated the law of constant proportions. In a chemical substance, the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In water, the ratio of the mass of hydrogen to the mass of oxygen is always one is to eight, whatever the source.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So if nine grams of water is decomposed, one gram of hydrogen and eight grams of oxygen are always obtained.

scenes.animation: A second card: ammonia, 'NH3', splitting into 'Nitrogen 14 : Hydrogen 3' by mass. A balance tilts with fourteen blue blocks on one side and three white blocks on the other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Similarly, in ammonia, nitrogen and hydrogen are always present in the ratio fourteen is to three by mass, whatever the method or source.

scenes.animation: Worked example on a blackboard, line by line: 'Q: H : O = 1 : 8 by mass. Mass of O2 needed to react completely with 3 g H2 = ?', '1 g H reacts with 8 g O', '3 g H reacts with 3 × 8 = 24 g O', 'Answer: 24 g oxygen'. A calculator character double-checks: '24 ÷ 3 = 8 ✓'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Try this. Hydrogen and oxygen combine in the ratio one is to eight by mass to form water. What mass of oxygen will react completely with three grams of hydrogen?

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: One gram of hydrogen needs eight grams of oxygen, so three grams needs three times as much!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Right. Three into eight is twenty-four grams of oxygen. Check it: twenty-four by three is eight, so the ratio is still one is to eight.

scenes.animation: Big question mark: 'Why do these laws work?'. A sepia portrait of John Dalton appears with a speech bubble 'Atoms!'. A yellow 'EXAM TIP' sticker: 'Name the law: conservation of mass (Lavoisier), constant proportions (Proust)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: These laws made scientists ask why elements combine this way. John Dalton answered with his atomic theory, which is our next topic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember which law goes with whom. Conservation of mass with Lavoisier, and constant proportions with Proust.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a water droplet icon. Points appear: '1. Elements in a compound are always in definite proportions by mass', '2. Water H : O = 1 : 8; ammonia N : H = 14 : 3', '3. 3 g H needs 24 g O'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: in a chemical substance, the elements are always present in definite proportions by mass.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: in water, hydrogen to oxygen is one is to eight, and in ammonia, nitrogen to hydrogen is fourteen is to three.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: use the ratio to scale up, like three grams of hydrogen needing twenty-four grams of oxygen.

scenes.animation: An old English schoolroom, 1808. A cartoon John Dalton, with a wooden ball in each hand, builds towers of coloured balls on his desk. Zippy peeks in through a time portal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Who's this gentleman playing with marbles?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's John Dalton. Those balls are his idea of atoms, and they explained both laws of chemical combination.

scenes.animation: Postulates appear on scrolls one after another with matching visuals: '1. All matter is made of very tiny particles called atoms, which participate in chemical reactions' (a sand pile zooming into balls); '2. Atoms are indivisible particles, which cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction' (a hammer bouncing off a ball).

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dalton's atomic theory says that all matter is made of very tiny particles called atoms, which participate in chemical reactions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Atoms are indivisible particles, which cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So when wood burns in a Lohri bonfire, its atoms don't vanish?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not one of them. They only rearrange into new substances, like carbon dioxide and water vapour, which float away into the air.

scenes.animation: More scrolls: '3. Atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties' (identical red balls); '4. Atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties' (red and blue balls of different sizes).

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So every oxygen atom is like every other oxygen atom, but an oxygen atom is different from a hydrogen atom.

scenes.animation: Final scrolls: '5. Atoms combine in the ratio of small whole numbers to form compounds' (two white balls snapping onto one red ball); '6. The relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound' (identical water molecules marching out of a factory).

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Atoms combine in the ratio of small whole numbers to form compounds.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So which postulate explains which law?

scenes.animation: Two arrows connect postulates to laws: 'Atoms cannot be created or destroyed' → 'Conservation of mass'; 'Relative number and kinds of atoms constant' → 'Constant proportions'. A yellow 'EXAM TIP' sticker appears. A small 'Fun fact' tag notes that atoms were later found to have smaller particles, covered in the next chapter.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Atoms cannot be created or destroyed. That explains the law of conservation of mass.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a compound. That explains the law of constant proportions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: this link between postulates and laws is asked very often. Quote the exact postulate.

scenes.animation: Recap board with Dalton's wooden balls. Points appear: '1. Matter is made of tiny, indivisible atoms', '2. Atoms of an element are identical; different elements differ', '3. Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: all matter is made of tiny atoms that cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: atoms of the same element are identical, and atoms of different elements differ in mass and properties.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: atoms combine in small whole-number ratios, and these ratios are fixed in a compound.

scenes.animation: Zippy builds a brick wall at a construction site near the school. Each brick is labelled 'atom' and the finished wall is labelled 'matter'. Zippy then tries to see a single atom with a magnifying glass and fails.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If atoms are the bricks of matter, why can't I see even one?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because atoms are very small. Their radius is measured in nanometres.

scenes.animation: A size ladder scales down: 'Watermelon', 'Grain of sand', 'Ant', then zooming to 'Hydrogen atom ~10⁻¹⁰ m'. A card: '1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One nanometre is ten to the power minus nine metre. A hydrogen atom has a radius of about ten to the power minus ten metre.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Even if we can't see atoms directly, modern techniques can produce magnified images of the surfaces of elements showing atoms.

scenes.animation: Dalton's round symbols flash by (a circle with a dot for hydrogen), then Berzelius replaces them with letters. Symbol cards flip: 'H Hydrogen', 'O Oxygen', 'C Carbon', 'Al Aluminium', 'Co Cobalt', 'Ar Argon', 'Fe Iron (Ferrum)', 'Na Sodium (Natrium)', 'K Potassium (Kalium)'. An 'IUPAC' stamp approves them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dalton was the first to use symbols for elements. Berzelius later suggested symbols made from one or two letters of the name.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Today, IUPAC approves the names and symbols. The first letter is always capital and the second is small, like aluminium, A l, and cobalt, C o.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some come from Latin names. Iron is F e from ferrum, sodium is N a from natrium, and potassium is K from kalium.

scenes.animation: An EXAM TIP card: 'Co = cobalt (element); CO = carbon monoxide (compound)'. The two stand side by side, the CO one splitting into C and O balls.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So Co and CO are the same thing, just shouting?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No! Co with a small o is cobalt, an element. CO with both capitals is carbon monoxide, a compound. Exam tip: capitalisation carries marks.

scenes.animation: A see-saw balance: a carbon-12 atom is sliced into 12 equal pieces; one piece is tagged '1 u = 1/12 of mass of a C-12 atom'. A table builds: 'H 1 u, C 12 u, N 14 u, O 16 u, Na 23 u, Mg 24 u, S 32 u, Cl 35.5 u, Ca 40 u'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Atoms are too light to weigh individually, so we use relative atomic mass. In 1961, carbon-12 was chosen as the standard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One atomic mass unit is a mass unit equal to exactly one-twelfth the mass of one atom of carbon-12. It is written as u.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So hydrogen is 1 u, carbon 12 u, nitrogen 14 u, oxygen 16 u, sodium 23 u, and chlorine 35.5 u.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a brick icon. Points appear: '1. Atoms are tiny: radius in nanometres', '2. IUPAC symbols: first letter capital, some from Latin (Fe, Na, K)', '3. 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: atoms are tiny, with radii measured in nanometres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: IUPAC symbols start with a capital letter, and some come from Latin names like ferrum and natrium.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: one atomic mass unit is one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

scenes.animation: A dance floor at a school fest. Some cartoon atoms dance alone (helium, argon), some pair up (O2, H2), and one group of eight sulphur atoms forms a ring. Zippy stands confused in the middle.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Some atoms dance alone and some in groups. Who decides?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each element does. Atoms of most elements can't exist independently, so they form molecules or ions.

scenes.animation: A definition card: 'Molecule: smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently and shows all its properties; two or more atoms chemically bonded'. Atoms click together with glowing bonds.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together, held by attractive forces.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It is the smallest particle of an element or a compound that is capable of independent existence and shows all the properties of that substance.

scenes.animation: An atomicity table builds: 'Monoatomic: He, Ar', 'Diatomic: H2, O2, N2, Cl2', 'Triatomic: O3 (ozone)', 'Tetra-atomic: P4', 'Polyatomic: S8'. Then compounds: 'H2O: H 1 : O 8 by mass', 'NH3: N 14 : H 3', 'CO2: C 3 : O 8'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The number of atoms in a molecule is its atomicity. Noble gases like helium and argon are monoatomic. Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine are diatomic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ozone is triatomic, phosphorus is tetra-atomic, and sulphur exists as S8, which is polyatomic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Molecules of compounds join atoms of different elements in a fixed ratio. In carbon dioxide, carbon and oxygen are in the mass ratio three is to eight.

scenes.animation: A sodium atom hands one electron to a chlorine atom; the sodium turns into 'Na⁺ cation' and chlorine into 'Cl⁻ anion'. They snap together into a sodium chloride crystal lattice. Label: 'Ion: charged species; cation positive, anion negative'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Compounds made of metals and non-metals contain charged species called ions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A negatively charged ion is an anion, and a positively charged ion is a cation. Sodium chloride is made of sodium cations and chloride anions.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So table salt is just a big hug between plus and minus!

scenes.animation: Polyatomic ion cards float in: 'NH4⁺ ammonium', 'OH⁻ hydroxide', 'NO3⁻ nitrate', 'HCO3⁻ hydrogen carbonate', 'CO3²⁻ carbonate', 'SO3²⁻ sulphite', 'SO4²⁻ sulphate', 'PO4³⁻ phosphate'. A yellow 'EXAM TIP' sticker: 'A polyatomic ion acts as one unit with a net charge'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A group of atoms carrying a charge is a polyatomic ion, like ammonium, hydroxide, nitrate, carbonate and sulphate.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: memorise these polyatomic ions with their charges. You will need them in the very next topic for writing formulae.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a dancing molecule icon. Points appear: '1. Molecule: smallest independent particle, atoms chemically bonded', '2. Atomicity: mono, di, tri, tetra, poly', '3. Ions: cation (+), anion (−), polyatomic ions'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: atomicity is the number of atoms in a molecule, from monoatomic to polyatomic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: ions are charged species; cations are positive, anions are negative, and some ions are groups of atoms.

scenes.animation: A cricket ground. Zippy writes 'Al O' on a scoreboard as the formula for aluminium oxide; a cartoon umpire raises a finger: 'OUT!'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Aluminium plus oxygen, so A l O. Why am I out?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because you ignored valency. A formula must balance the combining capacities of both elements.

scenes.animation: Atoms with little hands: hydrogen and chlorine with one hand each, oxygen with two, aluminium with three. A card: 'Valency = combining capacity of an element'. A table of ions builds: 'Na⁺, K⁺, Ag⁺ (1); Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺ (2); Al³⁺ (3); Cl⁻, Br⁻ (1); O²⁻, S²⁻ (2); N³⁻ (3)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The combining power, or capacity, of an element is its valency. Think of valency as the number of hands an atom can hold with.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rule one: the valencies or charges on the ions must balance. Rule two: with a metal and a non-metal, write the metal first. Rule three: if a polyatomic ion appears more than once, put it in brackets.

scenes.animation: Criss-cross method builds step by step for aluminium oxide: 'Al O' with valencies '3' and '2' written below; arrows cross over; subscripts drop in to give 'Al2O3'. Check line: 'Al: 2 × 3 = 6, O: 3 × 2 = 6 ✓'. Zippy's scoreboard updates to 'Al2O3'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use the criss-cross method. Write aluminium and oxygen, with valencies three and two below them. Cross them over.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Aluminium gets two, and oxygen gets three. So aluminium oxide is A l two O three.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Check it. Two aluminium atoms give two into three, six. Three oxygen atoms give three into two, six. Balanced!

scenes.animation: More examples build one by one: 'Hydrogen chloride: H(1) Cl(1) → HCl', 'Hydrogen sulphide: H(1) S(2) → H2S', 'Magnesium chloride: Mg(2) Cl(1) → MgCl2', 'Calcium oxide: Ca(2) O(2) → Ca2O2 → CaO (simplify)'. The Ca2O2 line is crossed out in orange and simplified.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Hydrogen chloride is H C l. Hydrogen sulphide is H two S. Magnesium chloride is M g C l two.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Calcium oxide: both valencies are two, so C a two O two!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Almost. When the valencies are equal, the formula simplifies to C a O.

scenes.animation: Polyatomic ions join: 'Calcium hydroxide: Ca(2) OH(1) → Ca(OH)2', 'Sodium carbonate: Na(1) CO3(2) → Na2CO3', 'Ammonium sulphate: NH4(1) SO4(2) → (NH4)2SO4'. Brackets glow when they appear. A yellow 'EXAM TIP' sticker: 'No brackets for a single polyatomic ion: NaNO3, not Na(NO3)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Calcium hydroxide is C a O H in brackets, two. Sodium carbonate is N a two C O three. Ammonium sulphate is N H four in brackets, two, S O four.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: use brackets only when there are two or more of the same polyatomic ion. Sodium nitrate is simply N a N O three.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the cricket scoreboard now showing 'Al2O3 ✓'. Points appear: '1. Valency = combining capacity', '2. Balance valencies with the criss-cross method; metal first', '3. Brackets for repeated polyatomic ions; simplify if possible'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: valency is the combining capacity of an element.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: balance the valencies using the criss-cross method, writing the metal first.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: bracket repeated polyatomic ions, and simplify the formula when you can.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Not out this time, umpire!

name: Molecular Mass and Formula Unit Mass

scenes.animation: A kirana shop. The shopkeeper weighs a water molecule on a tiny balance; a cartoon receipt prints '2 H + 1 O = ?'. Zippy reaches for a calculator.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If I know each atom's mass, can I get the bill for a whole molecule?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Just add up the atomic masses of all the atoms in it.

scenes.animation: A definition card: 'Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule (in u)'. Worked lines build on a blackboard: 'H2O = 2 × 1 + 1 × 16', '= 2 + 16 = 18 u'. Then 'HNO3 = 1 + 14 + 3 × 16', '= 1 + 14 + 48 = 63 u'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The molecular mass of a substance is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in a molecule. It is expressed in atomic mass units.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Water, H two O. Two hydrogens give two into one, which is two. One oxygen is sixteen. Two plus sixteen is eighteen u.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Nitric acid, H N O three. One plus fourteen plus three into sixteen. That is one plus fourteen plus forty-eight, which is sixty-three u.

scenes.animation: More molecules build on the board: 'C2H6 = 2 × 12 + 6 × 1 = 24 + 6 = 30 u', 'NH3 = 14 + 3 × 1 = 17 u', 'CH3OH = 12 + 3 × 1 + 16 + 1 = 32 u'. Each total gets a green check.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Let me try ethane, C two H six! Two into twelve is twenty-four, six into one is six. Thirty u!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Correct. Now methanol, C H three O H. Twelve, plus three, plus sixteen, plus one.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Twelve plus three is fifteen, plus sixteen is thirty-one, plus one is thirty-two u!

scenes.animation: A sodium chloride crystal lattice appears with no separate molecules. Card: 'Formula unit mass: for ionic compounds, sum of atomic masses of all atoms in a formula unit'. Worked lines: 'NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u', 'CaCl2 = 40 + 2 × 35.5 = 40 + 71 = 111 u'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ionic compounds like sodium chloride have no separate molecules, so we use formula unit mass. We calculate it in the same way.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sodium chloride is twenty-three plus thirty-five point five, which is fifty-eight point five u.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Calcium chloride is forty plus two into thirty-five point five. That is forty plus seventy-one, which is one hundred and eleven u.

scenes.animation: Board-exam style card: 'Given Zn = 65 u, Na = 23 u, K = 39 u, C = 12 u, O = 16 u'. Lines build: 'ZnO = 65 + 16 = 81 u', 'Na2O = 2 × 23 + 16 = 46 + 16 = 62 u', 'K2CO3 = 2 × 39 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 78 + 12 + 48 = 138 u'. A yellow 'EXAM TIP' sticker: 'Multiply subscripts first, then add'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A textbook exercise. Zinc oxide is sixty-five plus sixteen, eighty-one u. Sodium oxide is two into twenty-three, forty-six, plus sixteen, sixty-two u.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Potassium carbonate is two into thirty-nine, seventy-eight, plus twelve, plus three into sixteen, forty-eight. Total one hundred and thirty-eight u.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: multiply each atomic mass by its subscript first, then add. And always write the unit u.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the kirana receipt now reading 'H2O = 18 u'. Points appear: '1. Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses in a molecule', '2. Formula unit mass for ionic compounds (NaCl = 58.5 u)', '3. Multiply by subscripts, add, write u'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: for ionic compounds, we calculate formula unit mass the same way.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: multiply by subscripts, add carefully, and always write the unit u.
